newsitem.title: USA: Russia to unilaterally cut developing nation debt.
newsitem.headline: Russia to unilaterally cut developing nation debt.

text.p: Russia agreed to unilaterally slash its claims on developing country debtor nations by anywhere from 30 to 80 percent as part of a deal to gain entry into the Paris Club, a senior U.S. official said on Friday.

"This agreement represents the financial end of the Cold War," Deputy Treasury Lawrence Summers said. "Russia, along with the other creditor nations, will work together to address the debt problems of developing countries."

Russia had been pressing for some time to join the Paris Club of creditor countries, but difficulties in measuring the exact worth of the credits that Moscow had inherited from the Soiviet Union had kept it out.
The loans were denominated in rubles that were never traded freely against other currencies and much of the credits were for the purchase of military equipment.
Summers said that Russia's reduction in those claims, which will vary from country to country, reflect those difficulties.
The cuts will also take account of debt relief already granted by the Paris Club and the economic situation of the countries concerned, according to a fact sheet issued by the White House.
Summers said that Russia has a little more than $120 billion in claims outstanding. He said it was too soon to say how much of that will be reduced under Friday's agreement.

The reduction in debts agreed to by Russia on Friday is independent of any additional debt relief that the Paris Club may grant developing countries in the future. Summers said that some African nations may thus eventually see their debts to Russia reduced by as much as 90 to 95 percent.

"The agreement puts Russia on the same standing as the rest of the Paris Club," the White House fact sheet said. "It is an important part of this agreement that, consistent with Paris Club rules, Russia will not collect pariah debt while the Paris Club is not doing so."
